content: Epithelial membrane protein 3 (EMP3) is a transmembrane signaling molecule encoded by the EMP3 gene, which is part of the peripheral myelin protein gene family 22-kDa (PMP22). This family is primarily responsible for the formation of compact myelin sheaths. Although the precise functions and mechanisms of EMP3 remain unclear, it is hypothesized that EMP3 may be epigenetically linked to certain types of cancer. EMP3 is a protein consisting of 163 amino acids, and its gene is located on chromosome 19q13.3 in humans. Among various tissues, EMP3 is most highly expressed in peripheral blood leukocytes. Structurally, the protein contains four transmembrane domains and two N-linked glycosylation sites located in its first extracellular loop. Functionally, EMP3 is involved in cell-to-cell interactions and cell proliferation. Both overexpression and silencing of EMP3 disrupt its normal gene expression, which can lead to cancer development and progression. Based on its observed properties and prognostic studies in various cancers, EMP3 appears to have a tumor-suppressor-like role, regulating processes such as differentiation, apoptosis, and cancer cell development. However, the exact mechanisms underlying these functions remain to be elucidated. EMP3 in Tumorigenesis and Carcinogenesis Primary Breast Carcinomas The role of EMP3 in the development of carcinomas, including breast cancer, is not fully understood. However, studies have shown that EMP3 mRNA expression is significantly higher in primary breast carcinomas compared to normal breast tissues. Overexpression of EMP3 is strongly associated with histological grade III tumors, lymph node metastasis, and elevated Her-2 expression. Additionally, hypermethylation of the EMP3 promoter region has been observed in approximately 35% of breast carcinoma cases. Interestingly, high levels of EMP3 expression are present in breast cancer patients regardless of whether the promoter region is hypermethylated or unmethylated. Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, is primarily associated with chronic hepatitis B and C virus infections. In HCC, EMP3 expression is significantly higher in tumor cells compared to normal liver tissues from the same region. Paradoxically, patients with lower histological grades of HCC exhibit higher levels of EMP3 expression. Gene silencing (knockdown) of EMP3 in HCC cells has been shown to reduce cell proliferation and arrest the cell cycle, suggesting that EMP3 may play a tumor-suppressive role in this context. Brain Cancer EMP3 is implicated in the progression of neuroblastomas and glioblastomas, two aggressive and highly lethal types of brain cancer. In glioblastoma (GBM), EMP3 functions as an oncogene, with its overexpression correlating with tumor progression. Reducing EMP3 expression in CD44-high GBM cell lines induces apoptosis and inhibits tumorigenesis. A specific signaling pathway involving EMP3 in glioblastoma was identified in 2016: the TGF-β/Smad2/3 signaling pathway. Dysregulated TGF-β signaling promotes tumorigenesis in various human cells, particularly in CD44-high glioma cells. EMP3 interacts with the TGF-β receptor to regulate the activation of TGF-β/Smad2/3 signaling, ultimately suppressing cell proliferation and reducing tumorigenesis in glioblastoma. Clinical Significance The role of EMP3 in tumor suppression remains controversial, and no validated treatments targeting EMP3-related carcinomas currently exist for humans. However, animal studies have shown promising results, with modifications to the EMP3 gene leading to suppression of tumor growth in experimental models. Further research is needed to explore the therapeutic potential of targeting EMP3 in cancer treatment.
